title: China’s Weaponization of Dual-Use Research Vessels for Undersea Data Dominance
gist: Using AIS data on 223 research vessels from 2020-2025, CSIS's Futures Lab finds PRC-flagged research ships spend a statistically larger share of time near subsea cables on the high seas than fleets of 47 other nations, with a sharp rise in 2024. Case studies of Xiang Yang Hong 06 near Guam and Ke Xue across Western Pacific and Bering Sea cables show survey-like patterns away from mineral zones; the authors urge shared maritime domain awareness, joint patrols and allied cable-repair hubs.

themes.theme: Statistical evidence of PRC cable surveillance

insights.claim: PRC-flagged research vessels spend a statistically significantly larger share of time on the high seas near subsea infrastructure than research vessels from 47 other nations, including the US and Russia.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Raises perceived sabotage risk to trans-Pacific cables owned by US hyperscalers and carriers.
insights.locator: The PRC Exploits the High Seas for “Research”

insights.claim: PRC research vessel activity near subsea infrastructure rose sharply in 2024, when seven Chinese research vessels ranked above the 80th percentile for time spent near high-seas infrastructure.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Indicates escalating Chinese undersea ISR, a leading indicator for cable-security spending.
insights.quote: PRC activity was especially pronounced in 2024, when seven of its research vessels ranked above the 80th percentile for time spent near subsea infrastructure on the high seas.
insights.locator: The PRC Exploits the High Seas

insights.claim: The authors acknowledge their regression model explains only about 1.3 percent of variation in the data, and the China effect weakens in precision under more conservative error structures, though it stays significant.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The statistical signal is real but modest; treat claims of intent with caution.
insights.locator: Appendix A: Research Design and Methods

insights.claim: The authors argue the CCP is ramping up surveillance of the undersea infrastructure it would seek to sabotage in a future conflict, using civilian research vessels for plausible deniability under military-civil fusion.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Cable cuts are a credible first-move in a Taiwan contingency, a tail risk for Asian connectivity and markets.
insights.quote: Put simply, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is ramping up its surveillance of the very undersea infrastructure that it would undoubtedly seek to sabotage in a future conflict.

insights.claim: Undersea fiber-optic cables carry an estimated 99 percent of international data and about $22.4 trillion in daily transactions, and satellites cannot replace that bandwidth if cables are degraded.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Cable disruption would be a systemic financial and communications shock with no quick satellite substitute.
insights.quote: Undersea fiber-optic cables carry an estimated 99 percent of data internationally, and daily transactions are worth an estimated $22.4 trillion.

insights.claim: Cable repair delays are steadily increasing due to a shortage of repair ships and complex, often opaque international permitting processes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Repair-ship scarcity is an investable bottleneck and lengthens outage risk.

insights.claim: The US has a single dedicated cable repair ship that is more than 40 years old, supplemented by two chartered commercial vessels, and a single repair can cost $1 million to $3 million excluding crew costs.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Points to likely government spending on new cable-repair vessels and contracts.
insights.quote: For example, the United States’ single dedicated cable repair ship is more than 40 years old; its work is supplemented by two chartered commercial vessels.

insights.claim: US Navy officials testified in March 2026 that the PLA Navy uses temperature, salinity and current data to optimize sonar performance and support persistent underwater surveillance.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Oceanographic data collection is directly tied to submarine warfare capability.

themes.theme: Case studies: Guam and the Western Pacific

insights.claim: Between February and May 2024, Xiang Yang Hong 06 made three trips to the high seas about 210 nautical miles off Guam, surveying the Apricot and ASIA-America Gateway cables outside mineral-rich zones and outside the US EEZ.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Guam's connectivity, critical for US Pacific logistics, is being mapped by Chinese state vessels.
insights.locator: Case Study 1: Xiang Yang Hong 06 near Guam

insights.claim: None of the cable systems intersected by Xiang Yang Hong 06 is owned or operated by a PRC-based entity, suggesting deliberate surveying of foreign-built infrastructure.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Non-Chinese cable owners bear concentrated sabotage exposure.

insights.claim: In 2024 the Ke Xue surveyed near at least 10 subsea cable systems from the Western Pacific to the Bering Sea, including cables owned by Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon Web Services and AT&T, while avoiding mineral exploration regions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: US hyperscaler-owned trans-Pacific cables face rising security and insurance costs.

insights.claim: The Ke Xue surveyed about 150 nautical miles from Japan's Okinotori Island, which the authors judge was likely intended to normalize PRC rejection of Japan's EEZ claim there.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Adds a lawfare front to Sino-Japanese maritime tensions.
insights.locator: With these journeys, the Ke Xue challenged

insights.claim: The Ke Xue conducted survey-like movements near Russia's government-owned Polar Express cable and briefly turned off AIS near Shemya Island, home to US Eareckson Air Station, reappearing about 30 nautical miles away three hours later.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Suggests China surveils even its 'no limits' partner Russia and US Arctic staging sites.
insights.quote: This was an unexpected finding and likely reveals PRC interest in carrying out ISR on Russia’s subsea telecommunications infrastructure.
insights.locator: The Ke Xue’s activity in the Bering Sea

insights.claim: UNCLOS does not clearly define marine scientific research versus hydrographic or military surveys and does not prohibit persistent activity near undersea cables on the high seas, creating a legal gray zone China exploits.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: No legal tool currently constrains such surveys, so responses must be operational.
insights.quote: In effect, UNCLOS does not prohibit persistent activity near undersea cables.
insights.locator: The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea

insights.claim: The US views military and hydrographic surveys in foreign EEZs as lawful without consent, while China requires consent for such activity in its own EEZ, an asymmetry that complicates any reciprocal restriction.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Washington's own legal stance limits its ability to object to Chinese surveys.
insights.locator: The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea

insights.claim: The authors propose an International Countermaritime Gray Zone forum with European and Indo-Pacific working groups and a public dashboard naming private enablers such as insurers, shipping companies, banks and repair yards.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Could create reputational and sanctions risk for firms servicing gray zone fleets.
insights.locator: Establish international countermaritime gray zone forums

insights.claim: They recommend a US Coast Guard-led International Infrastructure Security Exchange for joint patrols near high-seas cables, and vetted contractor-owned multinational cable repair fleets with streamlined permitting.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Potential demand for cable-ship operators, maritime surveillance sensors and MDA analytics.
insights.locator: Form a multilateral coalition of maritime law enforcement

insights.claim: The authors argue countering dual-use gray zone activity cannot depend on proving intent behind each mission but must track cumulative long-term behavioral patterns across jurisdictions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Favors persistent AIS/satellite analytics providers over incident-based monitoring.
insights.quote: Countering dual-use gray zone activity therefore cannot depend on proving the intent behind each mission.
